# Exercise 4, part 1: the eight snippets, sorted

<!-- Generated by tools/build.js. Do not edit this file: change its source and run node tools/build.js. -->

This is a teaching key, not legal advice. An employer's own policy on AI tools comes first: where it is stricter, follow it.

## Fine to paste

### Snippet 1: Our price list, as published on our website

*Why someone might paste it:* To ask for help writing a short offer for new customers.

```text
Larkfield Wholesale price list
12 oz paper cups, carton of 1,000: $36.50
Lids for 8 to 16 oz cups, carton of 1,000: $18.00
Takeaway boxes, medium, carton of 250: $27.80
```

**Why:** It is already public: anyone can read it on the website. Nothing in it is about a person, and nothing is secret.

### Snippet 2: A paragraph for our website's news page, not yet published

*Why someone might paste it:* To ask for a clearer version.

```text
From April, every carton we send will be made from recycled board. Customers can give empty cartons back to our drivers, and we will use them again.
```

**Why:** It is your own text, written to be published. It names no one and holds nothing confidential.

## Paste after removing details

### Snippet 3: A customer's complaint, with her name, e-mail address and order number

*Why someone might paste it:* To ask for help with the wording of a reply.

```text
From: Mira Okafor, Halden Street Bakery <mira.okafor@example.com>
Subject: Re: Order SO-20417 has not arrived - short and damaged

The delivery came this morning at 10:30, thank you. But it is not right. We received 34 cartons of cups, not 40, so 6 are missing. And of the 34 that came, 6 were crushed and wet, and we cannot use them. The 20 cartons of lids are fine. I have attached photos of the damaged cartons.
```

**The key accepts:** Paste after removing details or Do not paste.

**Why:** Two piles are defensible. The wording of a reply does not depend on who she is: replace her name, her e-mail address and the business with stand-ins such as [CUSTOMER], then put the real ones back in your reply. The order number means nothing outside your own company's systems, so it may stay, as it does in part 2. What would tip it to "do not paste": an employer's policy that keeps all customer correspondence out of public tools, or a complaint whose content would still point to her, or hold something sensitive, once her name is gone.

### Snippet 4: The orders table: thirty rows with business names, contact people, phones and e-mails

*Why someone might paste it:* To ask which customers ordered most this quarter.

```text
Order | Order date | Customer business | Contact person | Phone | E-mail | Amount | Status
SO-20398 | 3 Feb | Halden Street Bakery | Mira Okafor | 000-000-0101 | mira.okafor@example.com | $640.50 | Paid
SO-20399 | 3 Feb | Copperleaf Catering | Jonas Arvidsen | 000-000-0102 | jonas.arvidsen@example.com | $1,184.00 | Paid
(28 more rows)
```

**The key accepts:** Paste after removing details or Do not paste.

**Why:** Two piles are defensible. The question needs the amounts and a way to tell customers apart, not their names, phones or e-mails. Leave those columns out, replace each business with a stand-in such as Customer 01, and map the answer back on your own computer: part 2 of this exercise does exactly that. What would tip it to "do not paste": an employer's policy that keeps all customer data out of public tools, whatever is removed.

### Snippet 5: The warehouse rota for next week, with staff names (invented)

*Why someone might paste it:* To ask for a fairer pattern of early shifts.

```text
Week of 10 March
Sam Ridley: Monday to Wednesday, 06:00 to 14:00
Ola Petrova: Monday to Friday, 14:00 to 22:00
Jakub Novak: Thursday to Saturday, 06:00 to 14:00 (back after sick leave, no lifting)
```

**The key accepts:** Paste after removing details or Do not paste.

**Why:** Two piles are defensible. The pattern of shifts can be planned with Staff A, Staff B and Staff C, once the names are out and the note about sick leave is out too: it is health information about a person, and it does not change the question. What would tip it to "do not paste": in a team this small, the pattern itself can still point to the one person who has just come back from sick leave.

## Do not paste

### Snippet 6: A note from an employee's doctor (invented)

*Why someone might paste it:* To ask for help planning his duties while he recovers.

```text
Fit note: Jakub Novak, warehouse. Lower back strain. Not fit for lifting over 10 kg until 31 March. Review in 3 weeks.
```

**Why:** It is health information about a person. In a team of a dozen people, taking out the name does not hide who it is. Ask in general words instead: "How can a small warehouse plan duties for someone who cannot lift for a few weeks?"

### Snippet 7: Our customer contact list: every contact name with a mobile number

*Why someone might paste it:* To ask for help putting it into one tidy format for a new phone system.

```text
Jonas Arvidsen, Copperleaf Catering, 000-000-0102
Tessa Moreau, Bramble Lane Cafe, 000-000-0103
Ravi Castellan, North Quay Deli, 000-000-0104
(24 more rows)
```

**Why:** The list is nothing but personal details: take them out and nothing is left to work on. To learn how to tidy such a list, paste two rows you have made up, then do the real list yourself.

### Snippet 8: The terms of a signed supply contract with an events customer (invented)

*Why someone might paste it:* To ask what a penalty clause means for us.

```text
Supply agreement with Juniper Hall Events. Prices fixed for 12 months. An 8% discount in any month above $5,000.00. A penalty of $250.00 for each late delivery. Both parties keep these terms confidential.
```

**Why:** They are terms you have signed to keep confidential, and the contract says so. Ask the question in general words instead: "What does a penalty clause for late delivery usually mean for a supplier?"
